sections.content:
From 1 September 2026, new police constables in England and Wales start on £32,255 a year at pay point 1, with chief constables able to start recruits at point 2 (£33,609). Pay rises with service to £52,015 at point 7, and officers in London and the South East receive additional allowances reflecting higher living costs.

In Scotland, new constables start at £34,001 from 1 April 2026. Policing remains one of the few public-sector careers where you can earn a degree while being paid, through the degree apprenticeship route, and overtime and shift allowances can add significantly to basic pay.

sections.content:
You do not need a degree to join. The PCEP (Police Constable Entry Programme) is a two-year route for non-graduates, while the PCDA (Police Constable Degree Apprenticeship) takes three years and awards a funded BSc in Professional Policing Practice alongside paid training. Graduates of any subject can take the two-year DHEP (Degree Holder Entry Programme).

All routes lead to the same warrant card and full constable powers. The choice depends on your qualifications and how you prefer to learn: classroom-based study, work-based apprenticeship, or an accelerated path if you already hold a degree.

sections.content:
Candidates must be 17 or older and 18 at appointment, with British or Commonwealth citizenship or indefinite leave to remain, plus at least three years of UK residency. A full UK manual driving licence with six months of experience is required when you start, and all candidates pass vetting, a medical, and the fitness test.

The national process has four stages: application, sift, online assessment, and a force interview. Tattoos on the face, hands, or neck that could cause offence will rule you out, and custodial sentences are a bar, though cautions are judged case by case. Allow four to six months from application to training.
